how-much-to-charge-to-replace-a-toilet.h.text:
← Toilet replacement bid calculator

How much to charge to replace a toilet

Plumbers get shopped on a published $249 installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the flange or the rough-in. A two-piece 12-inch swap on a good flange is a different job from a one-piece on a 10-inch rough-in with a rotten closet flange, a new shutoff, a bidet seat, and a haul-away.

Open the free toilet replacement bid calculator

Price the closet and the bowl, not the $249 dump

A toilet replacement is a closet, then a bowl, then how ready that flange is. Two-piece standard is a stack. Comfort-height is a taller bowl. One-piece is weight. Bidet-combo is a seat and a nearby GFCI. Swap-only pulls a working toilet and hooks the existing supply. New-supply is a shutoff. Flange-repair is a rotten closet. Full-reset is both.

Two-piece versus one-piece on the same closet

Homeowners usually start from the two-piece special, then ask whether comfort-height, one-piece, or a bidet seat is “a little more.” On the same closet and the same scope it is not a little more. One-piece buys a heavier bowl and a longer set. Bidet-combo is a seat and a GFCI. The calculator prices all four bowls on the closet you already counted so you can quote the upgrade instead of matching the two-piece number on a one-piece job.

Swap-only is not a flange-repair

The cheap special is almost always a two-piece on a 12-inch rough-in, no haul, no bidet, no flange work. A one-piece flange repair is a different crew hour. Matching an installed number on a rotten-flange job is how a sold toilet becomes a loss when the closet bolts and the extra trip eat the margin.

This is not a shower, a water heater, or a sewer line

A walk-in shower is tile, a slope, and glass. A water heater is a tank. A sewer-line replace is the lateral. Hydro-jetting is cleaning a line. Septic pumping is a tank lid. A well-pump is a well. A water-softener is salt. A sump-pump is a pit. This prices a toilet replacement: the bowl, the rough-in, the flange, and extras.

Customer-supplied bowls are not a free set

Owners also shop a second special: “I already bought it — just set it for $249.” Zeroing the fixture invoice drops the bid. The trip and the set stay. A wrong rough-in is a second trip. See should I install a customer-supplied toilet for the three-way comparison on the same closet.

Saturday is not the weekday bid

Owners also shop a third special: “Can you come Saturday? Same $249?” A weekday slot is the wage you already timed. Same-day while they stay home is the same wage on a slower set. After-hours is time-and-a-half plus a second dispatch because an overflowing toilet is not a stop you combine with a weekday route. See should I take a Saturday toilet call for the three-way comparison on the same closet.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the toilet replacement bid calculator. It is not a plumbing-code determination, a fixture specification, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to replace a toilet?

Charge from toilet count, bowl, rough-in, scope, and extras — not a published $249 installed special. A two-piece 12-inch swap on a good flange is a different job from a one-piece on a 10-inch rough-in with a rotten closet flange, a new shutoff, a bidet seat, and a haul-away.

Is a swap-only the same bid as a flange-repair toilet?

No. Swap-only pulls a working toilet, sets a new wax ring, and hooks the existing supply. New-supply is a shutoff and a supply line. Flange-repair is a rotten closet or an extender. Full-reset is both. Matching an installed special on a flange-repair job is how a sold toilet becomes a loss when the closet bolts and the extra trip eat the margin.

How do comfort-height, one-piece, and a bidet seat change a toilet price?

Two-piece standard is a stack. Comfort-height is a taller bowl. One-piece is weight. Bidet-combo is a seat and a nearby GFCI. Price all four on the same closet to see the upgrade — matching the two-piece special on a one-piece job is the losing bid. Haul-away, a wax-free seal, and a bidet seat do not live in a published installed dump.

Is this the same as a walk-in shower, a water heater, or a sewer line?

No. A walk-in shower is tile, a slope, and glass. A water heater is a tank. A sewer-line replace is the lateral. Hydro-jetting is cleaning a line. This prices a toilet replacement: the bowl, the rough-in, the flange, and extras.

    Common questions

    Why is a $165 toilet a $645 job?

    Because almost none of the cost is the fixture. On the defaults the toilet is $165 of a $644.71 price; the rest is 2.76 hours of loaded labor, a wax ring, a supply line, a $55 offset flange, the vehicle, overhead, and margin. This is the arithmetic to show a homeowner who has priced the same toilet at a big-box store and wants to know what the rest is for.

    Why is travel 1.11 hours for six miles?

    Because the trip is not just driving. The default allows a fixed turnout time plus a per-mile component, which together cover loading, parking, walking the fixture in, and getting back out — the real elapsed cost of attending a short job. On a 2.76-hour call, 40% of the paid time is arriving and leaving, which is exactly why a flat “one hour labor” quote loses money on small plumbing work.

    What is the $55 offset flange for, and do I always need one?

    No — it is in the defaults because it is the commonest surprise, not because every job needs it. It shifts the toilet slightly off the existing waste pipe centre when the new fixture rough-in does not match the old one, which happens most often on older homes with a 10-inch or 14-inch rough-in. Set it to zero when you have confirmed a matching 12-inch rough-in; leave it in when you are quoting sight-unseen.

    Is haul-away of the old toilet included?

    Not on the defaults, and neither is a bidet seat or a wax-free seal. Disposal is worth pricing rather than absorbing: many transfer stations charge for porcelain, and an old toilet left at the kerb is a complaint. Turn the option on when the customer expects the old unit to leave with you, which most do unless you have said otherwise in writing.

should-i-install-a-customer-supplied-toi.text:
← Toilet replacement bid calculator

Should I install a customer-supplied toilet?

Owners call with a box in the hallway: “I already bought the toilet. Can you just set it for $249?” That sounds like free margin because the fixture invoice left the bid. It did not leave the trip, the wax, the set hours, or the chance that the bowl is a 12-inch on a 10-inch closet.

Open the free toilet replacement bid calculator

Zeroing the bowl is not a free install

A plumber-supplied two-piece still carries the fixture invoice. An owner-supplied bowl that actually fits zeros that line and keeps the same set hours. On a typical 12-inch swap-only — $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, six miles — the plumber-supplied bid is in the mid-$500s. Zeroing a $165 bowl drops it, but the owner-supplied walk-away stays above $249. Taking the Facebook special to “just set what they bought” still loses money.

You supplyThey supply, it fitsThey supply, wrong rough-in
Bowl invoice in the bidYesNoNo
Set hoursSameSameSame, plus a callback
At $249 install-onlyLosesStill losesLoses more

Wrong rough-in is a second trip

Store shelves default to 12-inch. Plenty of closets are 10-inch or 14-inch. Setting the wrong bowl means an offset flange or a drive back to exchange it. Price that callback on the same closet before you agree. The calculator adds a starting second trip and a 10-inch offset kit on top of the rates you already typed.

How to use the comparison

Open the toilet replacement bid calculator, enter the closet you are standing in, and put their install-only number in “price you’re considering.” The who-supplies table scores that number against you-supply, owner-supplies-it-fits, and owner-supplies-wrong-rough-in. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to replace a toilet. Saturday overflow? See should I take a Saturday toilet call. It is not a plumbing-code determination, a fixture specification, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each supply path.

Common questions

Should I install a toilet the customer bought at a store?

Only after you price the set without the fixture invoice. Pulling their box is still a trip, a wax ring, and crew hours. A $249 install-only special often sits under that walk-away number even when the bowl is free to you.

Does a customer-supplied toilet make the $249 installed special profitable?

Usually not. Zeroing a $165 two-piece invoice drops the bid, but loaded labor, travel, wax, and overhead stay. On a typical 12-inch swap the owner-supplied walk-away is still above $249. A wrong rough-in adds a second trip and an offset flange.

What if the store-bought bowl is the wrong rough-in?

That is a second dispatch plus an offset flange or an exchange. Price that callback on the same closet before you agree to set whatever they rolled into the driveway. The calculator adds a starting callback trip and a 10-inch offset kit on top of your current rates.

should-i-take-a-saturday-toilet-call.htm.text:
← Toilet replacement bid calculator

Should I take a Saturday toilet call?

Owners call with a weekday number: “Can you come Saturday? The only toilet is overflowing. Same $249?” That sounds like the same closet. It is not the same crew day. After-hours is time-and-a-half. An overflowing toilet is not a stop you combine with a weekday route, so it is a second dispatch. Working around a family that still needs the bath on a weekday is the same wage on a slower set.

Open the free toilet replacement bid calculator

Saturday is not the weekday bid

A weekday slot still carries the wage you already timed. After-hours raises that wage to time-and-a-half and adds a starting second trip. On a typical two-piece 12-inch swap — $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, 6 miles — the weekday bid is $565.65. After-hours is $779.92. The walk-away jumps from $452.52 to $623.94. Taking $499 to “just do Saturday at the weekday number” covers the weekday slot and loses $124.94 after hours.

A one-piece flange repair loses even on the weekday

The Saturday special is more tempting when they already bought a one-piece and the flange is rotten. The weekday bid is $1,937.11. Same-day while they stay home is $1,968.51. After-hours is $2,287.56 and the walk-away is $1,830.05. Taking $249 to “just set what I bought, tonight” still loses money — even on the weekday.

This is not a customer-supplied bowl or a walk-in shower

Customer-supplied bowls are their fixture and an install-only number — see should I install a customer-supplied toilet. After-hours is when you can stand in the bathroom. A walk-in shower is a wet area, a slope, and glass. A kitchen backsplash Saturday is tile overtime in a kitchen they still cook in. This prices a toilet replacement.

How to use the comparison

Open the toilet replacement bid calculator, pick the cheap-special or losing-job preset, and put their Saturday number in “price you’re considering.” The access table scores that number against a weekday slot, same-day while they stay home, and after-hours / Saturday. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to replace a toilet. It is not a labor-law determination, a union scale, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each access window.

Common questions

Should I take a Saturday or after-hours toilet replacement call?

Only after you price time-and-a-half plus a second emergency dispatch. An overflowing toilet is not a stop you combine with a weekday route. A $249 Saturday special on a one-piece flange repair sits under that walk-away number even on a weekday slot.

Does a same-day only-toilet call change the bid?

Yes. Same wage, slower set and punch-list. On a typical two-piece 12-inch swap the same-day bid is $595.08 versus $565.65 when they can wait for a weekday slot.

Can I take the weekday $499 number on Saturday?

Usually not on the job they actually want. On a cheap two-piece swap the after-hours walk-away is $623.94. $499 covers a weekday slot and loses $124.94 after hours. On a one-piece flange repair, $249 still loses money even on the weekday.

vs-a-flat-installed-price.html.text:
← Toilet Replacement Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat installed price

“$249 installed” is not a price for a toilet replacement — it is a price for one specific scope and one good rough-in, quietly applied to every closet that calls in.

What a flat installed price is

A flat installed price is the fastest way to quote: read one number off a flyer or a search ad and apply it to the call. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — a two-piece standard bowl, swap-only, on a good 12-inch rough-in with no flange repair — and then reused for every call afterward, whether or not the next closet looks anything like the one the price was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the toilet count, scope (swap-only, new-supply, flange-repair, or full-reset), toilet type (two-piece, comfort-height, one-piece, or bidet combo), rough-in (10, 12, or 14 inch), haul-away, wax-free seal, and a bidet seat, plus your own crew wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It prices the scope, the toilet type, and the rough-in separately, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat installed price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same dollar figure whether the flange is good or the swap needs a repair kit and extra hours — even though a flange repair alone adds labor and a parts kit a good flange never needs. Prices scope separately from a starting kit for swap-only, new-supply, flange-repair, or full-reset, so a flange repair is never quoted off a swap-only price.
Has no line for the rough-in, regardless of whether it is the common 12-inch closet or a 10- or 14-inch that needs an offset flange. Prices the rough-in separately — offset hardware and extra set hours — on top of the scope, so an off-size closet is never folded into "the same toilet."
Prices every bowl at the same fixture invoice, with no line for the extra hours and cost a heavier one-piece or a bidet-combo needs to set carefully. Applies a toilet-specific starting kit (two-piece, comfort-height, one-piece, or bidet combo) to the set hours and fixture invoice, so a heavier bowl is never quoted at the cheap special's invoice.
Has no line for a haul-away, a wax-free seal, or a bidet seat, regardless of how many the job needs. Prices haul-away, wax-free seal, and bidet-seat hours and materials separately, so a job needing all three costs more than a bare swap on an empty closet.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat installed price would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two closets, the same job-blind price

Using this calculator's own shipped presets:

JobThis calculator's priceThe same $565.65 flat installed price, applied regardless of scopeGap
1 two-piece bowl, 12-inch rough-in, swap-only (the job this flat price was built on)$565.65 — $452.52 break-even$565.65 (same job, same price)No gap: this is the one job the flat price fits.
1 one-piece bowl, 10-inch rough-in, flange repair, haul-away, bidet seat$1,937.11 bid price; $1,549.69 break-even cost$565.65The flat price quotes $984.04 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $1,371.46 below the calculator's bid price.

Both rows use the $565.65 price the two-piece, 12-inch, swap-only job's own bid works out to. Applied flat to the one-piece, 10-inch, flange-repair job, that price does not just erode margin — it prices below the job's own cost to complete, even though both jobs are "one toilet." Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat installed price is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one closet it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat installed price skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat installed price get a toilet replacement quote wrong?

Because the cost driver is scope and rough-in, not "a toilet." A one-piece bowl on a 10-inch rough-in with a rotten closet flange, a new supply line, a haul-away, and a bidet seat needs flange-repair labor and a repair kit, offset hardware for the rough-in, a heavier and more careful set, and a bidet seat and its own hours that a two-piece swap on a good 12-inch flange never sees. A flat installed price charges all of that the same as the cheap special it was built on.

What does a flat installed price usually leave out entirely?

Flange repair, an offset rough-in, a heavier bowl, a new supply line, a haul-away, and a bidet seat. A rotten flange alone is not "a toilet" -- it is its own repair, priced in its own labor and its own kit -- and a job that needs an offset rough-in, a new supply, a haul-away, and a bidet seat is doing five things a bare swap-and-set is not. A flat installed number has no line for any of them.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets: a two-piece 12-inch swap-only job prices at $565.65, on a $452.52 break-even cost. Applying that same $565.65 flat installed price to a one-piece bowl on a 10-inch rough-in with a flange repair, a new supply line, a haul-away, and a bidet seat quotes $565.65 for a job whose own break-even cost is $1,549.69 -- a $984.04 loss before a dollar of profit, and $1,371.46 below the calculator's own bid price for that job.

Is a flat installed price ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same scope, same toilet type, a good 12-inch rough-in every time -- a flat price can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the price does not know which job it was built on and neither does the estimator until the flange and rough-in are actually checked.

Does this calculator know what fixtures or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local supply-house invoices or labor rates. It takes the toilet count, scope, toilet type, rough-in, haul-away, wax-free seal, and bidet seat, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat installed price skips, not a market survey.

Open the Toilet Replacement Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read how much to charge to replace a toilet.

vs-servicetitan.html.text:
← Toilet Replacement Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running a plumbing company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one toilet replacement cost, given its scope, its toilet type, and its rough-in, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving plumbing among other trades, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule techs, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one toilet job's toilet count, scope (swap-only wax-and-set, new-supply with a new shutoff, flange-repair on a rotten closet, or a full reset), toilet type (two-piece, comfort-height, one-piece, or bidet combo), rough-in (10, 12, or 14 inch), optional haul-away, wax-free seal, and bidet seat, plus your crew wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It turns that into the price, the price per toilet, the extra-work share of the job — the part a flat installed-price special leaves out — the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that floor. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a plumbing company and need scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, and job costing across every crew and every job.ServiceTitan, or a comparable field service platform — running a whole company is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this toilet replacement, given its scope, its toilet type, and its rough-in?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How much more does a flange-repair full reset cost than the swap-only cheap special on the same closet?This calculator's scope comparison, not a flat per-toilet price.
Does the haul-away, wax-free seal, or bidet seat still cover its own labor and material?This calculator's extras line items, shown as their own share of the job.
Is the price I'm about to quote still above my walk-away cost for this job?This calculator's compare-to-proposed-price check.
I need one shared account so my whole crew is scheduling, dispatching, and invoicing the same way.ServiceTitan, or a comparable field service platform.
How does the math behind a toilet-replacement bid actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. ServiceTitan is used through a subscription account.

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and a plumbing company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan and headquartered in Glendale, California, used by HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and other trades to run scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, and reporting across a business, sold as an ongoing subscription account. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from toilet count, scope (swap-only, new-supply, flange-repair, or full-reset), toilet type (two-piece, comfort-height, one-piece, or a bidet combo), rough-in (10, 12, or 14 inch), haul-away, wax-free seal, and a bidet seat, plus crew wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, it turns that into the price, the price per toilet, the extra-work share of the job, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, before any of it touches a business-management system. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A shop that already schedules techs, dispatches crews, and invoices across every job is better served by ServiceTitan or a comparable field service platform; a plumber who wants an instant, private answer to what one toilet replacement should cost from its scope and rough-in is in the right place here.

Does this calculator determine the code requirement or size the rough-in for me?

No. Hours and material rates are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a plumbing-code determination or a fixture specification. Whether a flange needs repair, whether a rough-in reads 10, 12, or 14 inch, and what a given closet actually needs are still a judgment call for the licensed plumber on site.
